facts.claim: Gravity's pull on a falling climber, a rope or falling ice: standard gravity.

versions.note: Defined by ISO 80000-3; the real pull is about 0.5% greater at the poles than at the equator.

facts.claim: How hard snow holds a body sliding over it in ski clothing, the coefficient of kinetic friction: the game uses it for a climber sliding after a slip, and for a rope lying on the ground.

versions.note: Three fabrics on snow, a ski overall and two race suits, on a linear tribometer: dry friction, highest on the roughest fabric.

source.title: Nachbauer et al. 2016, Kinetic Friction of Sport Fabrics on Snow (Lubricants) → Abstract

facts.claim: The gradients, the rise over the run, on which the energy cost of walking was measured: from 0.45 m down to 0.45 m up for each metre across, about 24°.

versions.note: Ten runners on a treadmill, walking and running at gradients from −0.45 to +0.45.

source.title: Minetti et al. 2002, Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes (J Appl Physiol) → Abstract

facts.claim: The energy walking on the level costs, for each kilogram of body mass and metre walked, at the speed that makes it least.

source.title: Minetti et al. 2002, Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes (J Appl Physiol) → Abstract

facts.claim: The energy walking up the steepest gradient measured, +0.45, costs for each kilogram of body mass and metre walked.

source.title: Minetti et al. 2002, Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes (J Appl Physiol) → Abstract

facts.claim: The energy walking down the steepest gradient measured, −0.45, costs for each kilogram of body mass and metre walked: a fifth of the way up it.

source.title: Minetti et al. 2002, Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes (J Appl Physiol) → Abstract

facts.claim: The least energy walking costs on any gradient, for each kilogram of body mass and metre walked: on a gentle way down, technique.walking-cost-least-gradient, half the level's.

source.title: Minetti et al. 2002, Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes (J Appl Physiol) → Abstract

facts.claim: The gradient on which walking costs least: 0.10 m down for each metre across, about 6°.

versions.note: The cost is reduced to its least at −0.10.

source.title: Minetti et al. 2002, Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes (J Appl Physiol) → Abstract

facts.claim: Steeper than this gradient, up or down, walking works the muscles at the efficiency of their contraction, concentric up and eccentric down: the work against gravity is most of the cost, so each metre of height costs about the same however steep. The game takes it from 0.15 up, and from the steepest measured down.

versions.note: The mechanical efficiencies of walking and running above +0.15 and below −0.15 attained those of concentric and eccentric muscular contraction.

source.title: Minetti et al. 2002, Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes (J Appl Physiol) → Abstract

facts.claim: The power a fresh typical client at sea level, at a steady pace and carrying nothing, walks on, in watts for each kilogram they move: the body scales it by the capacity the altitude leaves, 60% at 5,000 m, and by the pack, and a step goes as fast as it pays for on the ground's gradient (technique.walking-cost-*). Fitted with the fastest walk and the ladder speeds so that a steady first crossing of the Icefall, drawn at 1/12 of its length (route.drawn-scale) with its walls and crevasses at life size, takes about 3.8 hours with the climb eased (technique.uphill-cost-share), the faster half of the 3–7 the sources give, by a climber who never stops at an anchor but steadies themselves on blue ice and the long ladders (#190): 3.78.

The fastest a climber walks in crampons, in metres a second, whatever power they have to spare: down a slope and on the flat their footing holds them to it, so their steps take less of their power and tire them less. Fitted with the walking power and the ladder speeds so that the way down the Icefall takes about 2.5 hours, the 4 from Camp 2 to Base Camp shared between the Icefall and the Western Cwm as the way up's 5 and 3 are: 2.9, with the climb eased (technique.uphill-cost-share) and the careful steps on ice and ladders (#190).

The share of the climb's extra cost, a metre up a slope over a metre on the level (technique.walking-cost-*), that a stride pays in the game: a playability tuning, not a measurement, so that the slopes between the ladders don't crawl (#186). Up a slope a stride pays the level's cost and this share of the rest, so a slope never goes faster than the level, and the steeper it is the more the climb is eased: twice as fast up 20°. Fitted so that a careful typical client who never stops at an anchor crosses the Icefall in about 3.8 hours, the faster half of the 3–7 the sources give: 3.78, with the veteran at the shortest, 3, and the novice at the middle, 5. A player stops at every anchor to clip, so their own crossing is longer.

Up to this steepness snow costs a climber in crampons none of their footing (#190); steeper, the footing lost grows in a straight line to technique.footing-loss-steep at the steepest ground walked. Fitted to the Lhotse Face, about 30°, where a slip ends badly, and to the Icefall's 20° slopes, walked without a thought.

The footing a climber loses a second walking the steepest ground walked without a ladder, at a whole stride (#190): from technique.slip-free-steepness it grows in a straight line from none to this, and the climber gets it back as far as they're sure-footed (technique.footing-back-moving); with none left, they slip. Fitted so that a long steep stretch walked without a pause costs a slip, held by the rope when the climber is clipped: the lesson is the rope, not the footing.

How fast that fresh climber at sea level crosses a ladder laid flat over a crevasse, in metres a second. The ladders are drawn at life size on a section drawn at 1/12 (route.drawn-scale), so a ladder takes twelve times its real mountain minutes: fitted with the speeds up and down a wall so that the Icefall's twenty-one ladders, ten over crevasses and eleven up and down walls of 3 to 11 m, take about an hour and a half of the way up's hours together.

How fast that climber goes up a ladder stood against a wall, in metres a second; between flat and vertical, the speed falls in a straight line over the sine of the ladder's angle. Fitted with the crossing speed to the Icefall's hours.

How fast that climber comes down a wall a ladder stands against, in metres a second: three times as fast as up it, as down the fixed rope beside it (technique.down-a-fixed-rope asks how climbers go down one). Fitted with the crossing speed and the fastest walk to the Icefall's hours down, which go down 48 m of its walls and up 18.

The footing a climber on a ladder loses a second, whatever its angle, at a whole stride (#190): the rungs under crampons, before a crossing's bounce (technique.ladder-bounce-loss). Fitted so that a ladder up or down a wall costs a fresh climber nothing they don't get back, and a tired one hurrying up it little.

The footing a climber standing still gets back a second, at a steady pace's sure-footedness (#190): a pause steadies them. Fitted so that a few seconds' stop on blue ice or a bouncing ladder brings them back to steady, as the game's lesson goes: stop, steady yourself, go on.

The footing a climber gets back a second on the move, at a steady pace's sure-footedness (#190): less than standing, and more at the rest step's care, less at the faster pace's (body.rest-step-footing, body.faster-footing). Fitted so that snow, a ladder up a wall and a short ladder across cost a careful climber nothing, and blue ice and a long ladder across do.

The footing a climber walking bare blue ice on the level loses a second at a whole stride, in crampons (#190), on top of the steepness's: hard, polished glacier ice, which the Icefall shows in its steps and walls. Fitted so that a careful climber at the rest step crosses it, one at a steady pace slips after ten metres or so without a pause, and one hurrying slips in a few seconds.

How much more footing blue ice takes for each unit of the sine of its slope, up or down (#190): a slope of ice is worse than a flat of it. Fitted so that a careful climber has to stop and steady themselves on a slope of ice twenty metres long.

How hard bare blue ice holds a body sliding on it, as technique.snow-friction is snow's (#190): a slip on ice slides on where one on snow would stop. Fitted so that a slip on a gentle slope of ice ends in the crevasse below it unless a rope holds the climber.

How much a ladder across a crevasse bounces for each metre walked on it and each metre of its length (#190): a long one, lashed from three or four, sinks in the middle and bounces. It dies away (technique.ladder-bounce-damp), and takes footing from whoever is on it (technique.ladder-bounce-loss). Fitted so that a steady pace across a ladder of three sections, about 8 m, slips halfway over, the rest step crosses it, and two on it at once bounce it twice as hard.
The share of a ladder's bounce that dies away a second once nobody steps on it (#190): a ladder settles in about three seconds. Fitted with technique.ladder-bounce-excite.
The footing a climber on a bouncing ladder loses a second for each unit of its bounce (#190). Fitted with technique.ladder-bounce-excite.
The footing a climber has back as they get up from a slip (#190), shaken: half. They steady themselves as after any loss of it.

The speed a falling climber hits the ice at, in metres a second, past which the fall kills them (#190): a drop of about 7 m through the air onto ice. Fitted so that a fall into one of the Icefall's crevasses, over 45 m deep in places (route.icefall-hazards), kills, as the fifteen-storey fall from a ladder near Camp 1 did in 2012 (accidents.2012-ladder-fall), and a slip down a few metres of a wall's foot doesn't.

How fast a fresh climber at sea level, hanging on a fixed rope after a slip off a ladder or over a lip, climbs back up to where they slipped, in metres a second, at a whole stride (#190): hand over hand on the rope and the ladder's rails, crampons on the ice. Fitted so that climbing back the metre or two a clipped slip leaves them below takes a minute or two of the mountain's time, and tires them.

The minutes on the move after which a crampon not checked before setting off comes loose, on the next ladder (#196): a skipped check catches up with the climber about an hour out of Base Camp, not at once, as the fall from a ladder near Camp 1 in 2012 began with a crampon caught on a rung (accidents.2012-ladder-fall).
How sure-footed a loose crampon leaves a climber, as a share of what they'd be with it strapped tight (#196): on blue ice and a bouncing ladder they slip within seconds, until they kneel to refit it.
The minutes a climber takes to kneel and refit a loose crampon, its straps tightened again, standing on the ground (#196).

The hours after setting off at which a headlamp without fresh batteries dies (#196): from the 3 a.m. start (time.base-camp-departure), the climber goes on by starlight until dawn, the ice and the crevasses' lips unlit.
On Everest, climbers who had climbed on another peak of Nepal before summit more often than those who hadn't, and die no less often.

versions.note: 67.6% against 61.5% summited in 2006–2019, an advantage that has about halved in 25 years; deaths, the descent's too, independent of experience. The database records earlier Nepalese and border peaks, not other mountains.

source.title: Huey et al. 2020, Mountaineers on Mount Everest: Effects of age, sex, experience, and crowding on rates of success and death (PLoS One) → Results

facts.claim: The share of the speed on a ladder and clipped to a fixed rope of a climber who has never used crampons, a jumar or a ladder, against one with alpine climbs behind them, whom the ladder speeds and the walking power are fitted to. Fitted so that such a climber, as fit as the typical client, takes about the middle of the hours the sources give a first crossing of the Icefall, 5, where a typical client who never stops at an anchor takes 3.8: 5.0.

The same share for a climber who has climbed a 7,000 m or an 8,000 m peak. Fitted so that such a climber, as fit as the typical client, crosses the Icefall the first time in about 3 hours, the shortest the sources give it, and summits more often: they take less time on the ropes, not fewer risks (technique.experience-and-summits).

How far a cowstail reaches from the climber's harness to the fixed rope, in metres: how far from the rope they can clip, and how far past an anchor the rope lets them. Fitted so that a climber beside a ladder can reach the rope fixed along it.

How fast falling ice, an avalanche or a breaking snow bridge throws a climber it catches down the slope, in metres a second: a fall their rope holds if they're clipped. Fitted so that an unroped climber caught on a slope slides off it.

The fastest slide a climber can stop with the ice axe driven into the slope, in metres a second: self-arrest works in a slide's first moments or not at all. Fitted to the Lhotse Face, where a slip not stopped at once ends badly.
How far from their body a sliding climber can drive the ice axe into the slope, in metres: an arm and the axe. Fitted with the arrest speed to the Lhotse Face.

facts.question: At an anchor where one fixed rope ends and the next begins, in what order does a climber move their cowstails across, and are they ever clipped to neither rope?

How do climbers on the South route rig their cowstails: the jumar on one and a carabiner on the other, and how long is each, so how far can a climber reach to clip? The game gives a cowstail 0.8 m of reach.

How does a climber cross a ladder laid over a crevasse in the Icefall: clipped to what, stepping how in crampons, and how fast? The game crosses at 0.6 m/s at sea level, less at altitude, and a long ladder bounces under a hurried step until the climber loses their footing.

How does a climber go up a ladder stood against an ice wall: clipped to what, and what holds a slip? The game climbs at 0.3 m/s at sea level and comes down at 0.9, as fast as down the rope beside it, less at altitude.
How does a climber go up a fixed rope on a jumar, on the Lhotse Face for instance: the rhythm of hand, feet and breath, and when does the second cowstail move?
How does a climber go down a fixed rope: abseiling on a belay device, with the rope wrapped round an arm, or on the carabiner alone, and where on the South route is each used?
What is the rest step, with its rhythm of steps and breaths, and how does the rhythm change with altitude and with bottled oxygen?
On hard, steep ice such as the Lhotse Face, where a fixed rope is in place: how are the crampons placed, on the front points or flat-footed, and when does the ice axe go in?

How fast does a climber walk on ground of each steepness, up and down, in crampons and with a pack, and how much slower on a ladder? The game's walking costs what Minetti et al. measured on a treadmill, read as rise over run, from 24° down to 24° up, each metre of height costing the same past that up to 60°; a climber walks on 2.2 W/kg at sea level, before the altitude and the pack take their share, and no faster than 0.7 m/s whatever they have to spare. The power, the fastest walk and the ladder speeds are fitted to the hours the sources give the Icefall, up and down, not measured.

How often does a climber slip on snow and ice of each steepness, and on a ladder, and how much does a careful pace help? The game takes no footing on snow up to 30°; at a steady pace a climber loses all of it in about 10 seconds of walking at 60°, and in about 20 seconds on level blue ice, while the rest step crosses both; a long ladder bouncing under a hurried step costs it in a few seconds (#190).

Up to what speed can a sliding climber stop themselves with the ice axe, on snow and on hard ice, and within how many seconds of the slip? How far from the body does the axe reach, and how hard do snow and hard ice hold a sliding climber without it? The game stops a slide no faster than 5 m/s, with the axe driven in within 1.5 m above the body, and never in the air; without the axe, a slide stops by itself only on ground gentler than about 19°, by the friction measured for ski fabrics on snow.

How much slower on the Icefall's ladders and fixed ropes is a client who has never used crampons, a jumar or a ladder than one with alpine climbs behind them, and how much faster one who has climbed a 7,000 m or an 8,000 m peak? Do they slip more, or less, for each metre? The game fits their speed there to the spread of the sources' hours for a first crossing, and leaves their slips for each metre as they are: experience brings more summits, not fewer deaths.
